question.prompt:
The figure is constructed from \(11\) line segments, each of which has length \(2.\) The area of pentagon \(ABCDE\) can be written as \(\sqrt m+\sqrt n,\) where \(m\) and \(n\) are positive integers. What is \(m+n?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2021_AMC_12B_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Since all eleven segments have length \(2\), first look for equilateral triangles. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the left and right unlabeled black points, respectively.

[Figure 1](figures/2021_AMC_12B_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

The drawn segments show that \(ABQ\) and \(CBQ\) are equilateral triangles on opposite sides of \(BQ\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(BQ\). In an isosceles triangle, the altitude from the vertex bisects the base, so both \(AM\) and \(CM\) are perpendicular to \(BQ\). Therefore \(A,M,C\) are collinear, with \(M\) between \(A\) and \(C\). Since \(BM=MQ=1\), the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
AM=CM=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3.
\]
Thus \(AC=2\sqrt3\). Also, \(BM=1\) is the height from \(B\) to \(AC\), so
\[
[ABC]=\frac12(2\sqrt3)(1)=\sqrt3,
\]
where brackets denote area.

Similarly, \(AEP\) and \(DEP\) are equilateral triangles on opposite sides of \(EP\). Applying the same midpoint-and-altitude argument gives
\[
AD=2\sqrt3,
\qquad [ADE]=\sqrt3.
\]
Now draw diagonals \(AC\) and \(AD\), dividing the pentagon into the three triangles \(ABC\), \(ACD\), and \(ADE\), with disjoint interiors.

Triangle \(ACD\) is isosceles, with equal sides \(2\sqrt3\) and base \(CD=2\). Its altitude from \(A\) bisects \(CD\), so its height is
\[
\sqrt{(2\sqrt3)^2-1^2}=\sqrt{11}.
\]
Hence \([ACD]=\frac12(2)(\sqrt{11})=\sqrt{11}\). Adding the three areas gives
\[
[ABCDE]=\sqrt3+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt3
=\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{11}.
\]
Thus \(m+n=12+11=\boxed{23}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Find the heights using equilateral triangles
